summary: VRChat is a social virtual world platform built on the Unity game engine, where both worlds and avatars are authored in Unity and uploaded. Nothing that goes in ever comes out: an upload is compiled into a Unity asset bundle tied to one pinned editor version and one target platform, so the same avatar must be built and uploaded separately for computers, standalone headsets and phones, and no tool outside a matching VRChat client can open the result. World rules are written in VRChat's own language, which compiles to VRChat's own bytecode and which VRChat states follows no version of the C sharp standard, so interactivity cannot travel with an asset either. What VRChat does unusually well is bounding guest content: two published closed lists of permitted components, hard numeric limits on network traffic, downloads and avatar size, and a published avatar scoring system that lets a viewer refuse anything too expensive. The one genuinely open interface is Open Sound Control, where a program on the same machine can set and read avatar values, push in gaze and body tracker poses and drive movement, with VRChat advertising itself for discovery over Zeroconf and asking the person's consent before it sends anything out. Two traps for a standards reader: the coordinate convention is left-handed with Y up, the opposite of the neutral transfer formats, and saved player data is forbidden by design from being shared between worlds, so a portal carries your account and your avatar and nothing else.

coverage.note: VRChat renders through the Unity game engine, and the evidence points to Unity's older "built-in" renderer rather than either of Unity's newer pipelines: the allowlist of components a world may contain includes Projector, Halo, LensFlare and FlareLayer, which only exist in the built-in renderer, and the supported add-on list names Post Processing Stack v2, which is also built-in-only. No VRChat page states the pipeline by name, and creators cannot add or reorder render passes.

coverage.note: This is the single largest interoperability problem. A VRChat world or avatar is not shipped as a model file at all — the upload tool converts the Unity scene into a Unity asset bundle, a compiled binary keyed to one pinned Unity editor version and to one target platform. Separate bundles must be built and uploaded for Windows, for Android and for iOS. Nothing outside a matching Unity build can open the result, and there is no way to get an asset back out. VRChat reads FBX at authoring time inside Unity; it writes nothing any other tool can read.

coverage.note: Clear and simple: one person owns each networked object and only that person may change its shared values. The first person into an empty instance owns everything not otherwise assigned. Ownership can be requested and transferred, and a script can approve or refuse the request. There is no server-authoritative option — authority always sits on somebody's computer.

coverage.note: VRChat plainly has a working transport, but it publishes nothing about it. Across every networking page checked — the overview, the specifications page, ownership, events, late joiners, components, performance and debugging — no protocol, port, framing or handshake is named. No independent client can join a VRChat instance, and no other system can speak to one. The only transport VRChat does document is Open Sound Control over the local machine, which carries a person's own avatar and tracking values, not session traffic.

coverage.note: No verifiable credential format of any kind. Nothing in VRChat's documentation index mentions credentials, decentralised identifiers or signed claims about a person.
There is no protocol for two parties to request and present claims about a person. All trust signals are read from VRChat's own servers by VRChat's own client.

VRChat has a real permission model — a ladder of trust ranks, per-rank shields that decide which parts of a stranger's avatar you will render, and a mutual consent rule before two people's avatars may touch each other. It is entirely internal: no party other than VRChat can read or verify what a given person is permitted to do.

VRChat computes its own pinch detection from fingertip distances.

coverage.note: Gaze can be fed into VRChat from any program over Open Sound Control, at documented named addresses, in several formats — a pair of angles, angles plus a focus distance, direction vectors, or separate values per eye — plus a single closed-ness value driving both eyelids. VRChat states the sign conventions and the ten-second timeout after which it reverts to automatic looking. On the privacy side, VRChat requires the person to consent before it starts sending tracking data out to a discovered companion program. The flow is inbound: outside programs push gaze into VRChat, and VRChat publishes no general gaze feed back out.

coverage.note: World rules are written in Udon, which is VRChat's own language running on VRChat's own bytecode interpreter. Creators usually write a restricted dialect of C# which the tool compiles down to Udon assembly, and VRChat states plainly that this dialect follows no version of the C# standard. Generic classes, interfaces, method overloads and properties do not work. The compiled program only runs inside VRChat and can never be moved to another runtime. The compiler itself is open source under a permissive licence, which is a real positive, but it only ever emits VRChat bytecode.

coverage.note: This is VRChat's strongest capability. Guest content cannot run arbitrary code: worlds and avatars may only use components from two published closed allowlists, anything else is refused at upload, and all scripting goes through the interpreter rather than the host runtime. Reaching the network is gated by an address allowlist that a person must deliberately override. On top of that sits the trust and shield system that decides how much of a stranger's avatar to render at all.
